structures.title: Basic word order with dropped subject
structures.explanation: Italian follows Subject-Verb-Object order, but the subject pronoun is normally omitted because the verb ending already shows the person. Use the pronoun only for emphasis or contrast.

structures.title: Forming yes/no questions
structures.explanation: The most common way to ask a yes/no question is to keep statement word order and raise your intonation. In writing only the question mark changes. Inversion exists but is far less used than in English.

structures.title: Negating a sentence
structures.explanation: Place non directly before the verb. Italian requires double negatives: non...niente (nothing), non...nessuno (nobody), non...mai (never), where both parts are kept.

structures.title: Saying what is happening right now
structures.explanation: Use stare plus the gerund to stress an action in progress at this moment. The gerund ends in -ando for -are verbs and -endo for -ere/-ire verbs. For the general present, the simple present is preferred.

structures.title: Expressing obligation (must / have to)
structures.explanation: Modal verbs like dovere (must), potere (can) and volere (want) are followed by an infinitive. Dovere expresses necessity or obligation and the following verb stays in the infinitive.

structures.pattern: Mi piace + singolare / Mi piacciono + plurale
structures.title: Expressing what you like
structures.explanation: Piacere works like 'to be pleasing to'. The thing liked is the grammatical subject, so the verb is singular (piace) with one thing or an infinitive, and plural (piacciono) with several. The person is an indirect pronoun (mi, ti, gli...).

structures.title: Pointing something out: here is / are
structures.explanation: Ecco presents or points to something or someone, for both singular and plural. It often fuses with pronouns: eccomi (here I am), eccolo (here it is), ecco a te (here you go).

structures.title: Real conditions (first conditional)
structures.explanation: For real, likely conditions, use se plus the present in the if-clause and the present or future in the main clause. Word order is flexible: either clause may come first.
structures.ex1_ref: If I have time, I'll come.
structures.ex2_ref: If it rains, we'll stay home.

structures.title: Comparing two things
structures.explanation: Use più (more) or meno (less) before the adjective, then di before a noun or pronoun. Use che when comparing two adjectives, two verbs, or after a preposition.
structures.ex1_target: Marco è più alto di me.
structures.ex2_target: È più facile leggere che parlare.
structures.ex2_ref: It's easier to read than to speak.

structures.title: Joining clauses with 'that/who'
structures.explanation: Che is the all-purpose relative pronoun for both subject and object ('who, which, that') and never changes form. After a preposition, use cui instead of che.
structures.ex1_target: L'uomo che abita qui è medico.
structures.ex1_ref: The man who lives here is a doctor.
structures.ex2_target: Il libro che leggo è interessante.
structures.ex2_ref: The book that I'm reading is interesting.

structures.title: Wanting someone else to do something
structures.explanation: When the two clauses have different subjects, verbs of wish, opinion, or emotion require the subjunctive after che. With the same subject, use the infinitive instead (Voglio venire).

structures.title: Saying there is / there are
structures.explanation: Use c'è with a singular noun and ci sono with a plural noun to state existence or presence. The past forms are c'era (there was) and c'erano (there were).

structures.title: Forming the passive voice
structures.explanation: The passive is essere plus the past participle, which agrees with the subject in gender and number. The agent, when named, is introduced by da.
structures.ex1_target: Il libro è stato scritto nel 1990.
structures.ex2_target: La cena è preparata da mia madre.
structures.ex2_ref: Dinner is prepared by my mother.

structures.title: Reporting what someone said
structures.explanation: Introduce reported statements with dire che. Tenses shift back: a present becomes the imperfect, and a future becomes the past conditional (sarebbe venuto).
structures.ex2_target: Ha detto che sarebbe arrivato tardi.
structures.ex2_ref: He said he would arrive late.

structures.title: The most / the -est in a group
structures.explanation: The relative superlative uses the definite article plus più or meno plus the adjective, with the group introduced by di. The article agrees with the noun in gender and number.
structures.ex1_target: È il più alto della classe.
structures.ex1_ref: He is the tallest in the class.
structures.ex2_target: È la città più bella d'Italia.
structures.ex2_ref: It's the most beautiful city in Italy.

structures.title: Expressing purpose (in order to)
structures.explanation: To express purpose or goal, use per followed by the infinitive. It answers 'why?' or 'what for?' and is used when both actions share the same subject.
structures.ex1_ref: I study in order to learn.
